claim: The overall pattern of DsRedE expression is highly consistent between embryos, being restricted to the most ventroanterolateral region of the placode until 19 hpf and expanding posteromedially at around 20.5 hpf.
source: The overall pattern of DsRedE expression is highly consistent between embryos, being restricted to the most ventroanterolateral region of the placode until 19 hpf and expanding posteromedially at around 20.5 hpf (Figure 1A and B; Videos 1 and 2).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 1A and B and Videos 1 and 2

claim: DsRedE expression pattern recapitulates the endogenous spatiotemporal pattern of neurog1 as analysed by in situ hybridisation.
source: This DsRedE expression pattern recapitulates the endogenous spatiotemporal pattern of neurog1 as analysed by in situ hybridisation (ISH) (Radosevic et al., 2014; Vemaraju et al., 2012; Andermann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by comparison with published ISH data from cited references

claim: DsRedE expressing cells delaminate and are incorporated into the SAG.
source: Moreover, DsRedE expressing cells delaminate (Figure 3H; Videos 1 and 11) and are incorporated into the SAG (Figure 1A and B; Video 3), supporting the use of this line to analyse single cell dynamics of neuronal specification.
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figures 1A, 1B, 3H and Videos 1, 3, and 11

claim: By 19 hpf, the neurogenic domain region accumulated more cells (15.4 ± 0.4% of the total number of cells in the vesicle, 49 ± 3 cells of 311 ± 16 cells respectively) than other regions (mean non-neurogenic region: 12.0 ± 0.1%, 36 ± 2 cells).
source: By 19 hpf, the neurogenic domain region accumulated more cells (15.4 ± 0.4% of the total number of cells in the vesicle, 49 ± 3 cells of 311 ± 16 cells respectively) than other regions (mean non-neurogenic region: 12.0 ± 0.1%, 36 ± 2 cells, Figure 1E)
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1E

claim: The neurogenic domain presented higher cellular density (2.16 ± 0.03 nuclei/1 × 10³ μm³) compared to mean non-neurogenic region (1.60 ± 0.03 nuclei/1 × 10³ μm³).
source: and presented higher cellular density (Figure 1F; neurogenic region: 2.16 ± 0.03 nuclei/1 × 103 μm3, mean non-neurogenic region: 1.60 ± 0.03 nuclei/1 × 103 μm3).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 1F

claim: Cell proliferation is highly enriched in the neurogenic region, with about 41% of the total number of divisions occurring in this domain.
source: Quantification of all the mitotic events inside the vesicle between 14 and 18.5 hpf revealed that cell proliferation is also highly enriched in this region (Figure 1G). While the increase in cell number in the neurogenic domain was moderate (about 3% more cells than other regions), the enrichment in mitotic events led to about 41% of the total number of divisions to occur in this domain.
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements of mitotic events shown in Figure 1G

claim: Already at 13 hpf there are rows of DsRedE expressing cells lateral to the neural tube and anterior to the epithelializing otic placode.
source: While it has been reported that neurog1 expression in the otic placode begins at 15 hpf (Radosevic et al., 2014), we found that already at 13 hpf there are rows of DsRedE expressing cells lateral to the neural tube and anterior to the epithelializing otic placode (Figure 2A; Video 4).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figure 2A and Video 4

claim: DsRedE expressing cells at 13 hpf coincide with neurog1 expressing cells detected by ISH.
source: These cells coincide with neurog1 expressing cells detected by ISH (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and previously assumed to belong to the anterior lateral line placode (Andermann et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by comparison with ISH data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and cited reference

claim: Some neurog1 expressing cells anterior to the otic placode migrate posteriorly and become incorporated into the anterolateral region of the otic epithelium.
source: Unexpectedly, when we followed these cells we found that some of them migrate posteriorly and become incorporated into the anterolateral region of the otic epithelium, in a position corresponding to the neurogenic domain (red brackets in Figure 2B; Video 5).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2B and Video 5

claim: Photoconverted Eos protein in nuclei anterior to the otic epithelium at 13 hpf was detected inside the vesicle at 20 hpf, confirming cell ingression.
source: To confirm this cell ingression, we injected NLS-Eos mRNA at 1 cell stage to obtain a homogeneous nuclear staining with the photoconvertable protein throughout the embryo. At 13 hpf, we photoconverted Eos protein (from green to red fluorescence) in a group of nuclei anterior to the otic epithelium where the migrating cells are located. At 20 hpf, we detected photoconverted nuclei inside the vesicle (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by photoconversion experiment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: A second pool of neurog1+ cells in the anterior region moves posteromedially without ingressing, remaining in the region of the SAG.
source: We also detected in the same anterior region a second pool of neurog1+ cells (expressing also neurod1; Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) that moves posteromedially without ingressing, remaining in the region of the SAG (blue brackets in Figure 2B; Video 5).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, and Video 5

claim: neurog1 expression is not sufficient for cell ingression.
source: These observations suggest that neurog1 expression is not sufficient for cell ingression.
evidence: Inferred from observation that some neurog1+ cells do not ingress

claim: neurog1 expression is not required for cell ingression.
source: Additionally, neurog1 expression was not required for cell ingression, as some neurog1- cells ingress. Consistently, we detected cell ingression events in neurog1 mutant embryos (neurog1hi1059, Figure 2—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: Supported by observation of ingression in neurog1 mutant embryos shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1G

claim: Some cells activate neurog1 expression while moving towards the epithelium and before their epithelialisation.
source: Interestingly, 3D tracking of individual cells of the ingressing pool revealed that some cells activate neurog1 expression while moving towards the epithelium and before their epithelialisation (Figure 2C; Video 6).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2C and Video 6

claim: Immediately after ingressing into the neurogenic domain, cells divide and delaminate, undergoing a complete cycle of epithelialisation and de-epithelialisation in only a few hours.
source: Immediately after ingressing into the neurogenic domain, these cells divide and delaminate, thus undergoing a complete cycle of epithelialisation and de-epithelialisation in only a few hours.
evidence: Inferred from tracking data of ingressing cells

claim: The migration of ingressing cells is a directional process occurring in individual cells.
source: Analysis of the movement of these cells suggests that their migration is a directional process occurring in individual cells (Figure 2D,E and F; Video 7; some cells of the same region migrate in other directions).
evidence: Supported by analysis of cell tracking data shown in Figure 2D, E, F and Video 7

claim: The leading front of ingressing cells periodically protrudes, followed by a rapid forward translocation of the nucleus.
source: We also observed that the leading front of cells periodically protrudes, followed by a rapid forward translocation of the nucleus (Figure 2G; insets of Video 7), as has been described during fibroblast migration (Petrie and Yamada, 2015).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figure 2G and Video 7, and comparison with cited reference

claim: The otic placode is only epithelialised medially at early stages, with the posterior part segregating from surrounding cells before the anterior region.
source: As we previously reported, the otic placode is only epithelialised medially at these stages (Hoijman et al., 2015). As epithelialisation progresses, at 14 hpf the posterior part of the placode is segregated from the surrounding cells, while the anterior region of the placode is not (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Video 8).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Video 8, and cited reference

claim: The posterior part of the placode folds approximately 3 hr before the anterior one.
source: Thus, the posterior part folds approximately 3 hr before the anterior one (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Video 8).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and Video 8

claim: The basal lamina at early stages is only rudimentary and not continuous.
source: Moreover, the basal lamina at these early stages is only rudimentary and not continuous (contrary to the one present at later stages surrounding the whole organ; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by laminin staining shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1E

claim: Cells activate neurog1 expression within the neurogenic domain through a process called 'local specification'.
source: We next evaluated if, in addition to ingressing cells, other cells start to express neurog1 within the neurogenic domain. We visualised the activation of neurog1 expression inside the otic vesicle in real-time (Figure 3A; Video 9), a process that we refer to as 'local specification'.
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A and Video 9

claim: The rate of increase in DsRedE signal is variable among cells (mean rate ranging between 0.15 and 0.54 a.u./min).
source: Dynamic quantification of DsRedE fluorescence levels in individual cells (Fcell) indicated that the rate of increase in the signal is variable among cells (Figure 3B, mean rate of increase ranging between 0.15 and 0.54 a.u./min, n = 11 cells).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: Cells begin to delaminate when DsRedE signal reaches a critical level (between 45.5 and 52.5 a.u.).
source: However, we found that when the signal reaches a critical level (between 45.5 and 52.5 a.u. in Figure 3B, gray region with red dots), cells begin to delaminate (visualised by the movement of the cell body to the basal domain of the epithelium).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B

claim: Cells delaminate relative to neurog1 levels and not to the time elapsed since they initiated neurog1 expression.
source: This suggests that cells delaminate relative to neurog1 levels and not to the time elapsed since they initiated neurog1 expression (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: Inferred from quantitative measurements shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Every cell divides only once in the 7 hr period analysed (n = 27/27).
source: To address this, we performed a 4D analysis of cell divisions and found that every cell divides only once in the 7 hr period analysed (n = 27/27).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data

claim: Mitotic cells are found either contacting the central lumen or apposed to a Pard3 scaffold perpendicular to the central luminal surface.
source: Mitotic cells are found either contacting the central lumen (Figure 3D) or not (peripheral divisions) (Figure 3E). Interestingly, these latter cells are apposed to an accumulation of the apical determinant Pard3 that forms a scaffold perpendicular to the central luminal surface of the vesicle, running from the lumen to the periphery (Figure 3F; Video 10).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figures 3D, E, F and Video 10

claim: All divisions in the neurogenic domain have the cleavage plane perpendicular to the apical surface regardless of their position in the epithelium or their neurog1 expression.
source: We observed that all divisions in the neurogenic domain have the cleavage plane perpendicular to the apical surface regardless of their position in the epithelium or their neurog1 expression (Figure 3G and H).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figures 3G and H

claim: All divisions in the neurogenic domain are symmetric, with both daughter cells delaminateing after division (27/27).
source: When analysing the fate of the daughter cells after division, we found all were symmetric (27/27): both daughter cells delaminate after division (20/27 delaminate during the timeframe analysed, 7/27 are positioned to delaminate at the end of the acquisition).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data

claim: Division can occur either before (13/25) or after (12/25) the induction of neurog1 expression.
source: However, division can occur either before (13/25) or after (12/25) the induction of neurog1 expression.
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data

claim: Daughter cells from mitoses of neurog1+Hi cells rapidly delaminate, remaining in close contact as they move to the periphery of the tissue.
source: Interestingly, daughter cells from mitoses of a neurog1+ cell with high levels of DsRedE expression (neurog1+Hi cell) rapidly delaminate, remaining in close contact as they move to the periphery of the tissue (Figure 3I and J; Video 11).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in imaging data shown in Figures 3I, J and Video 11

claim: Ablation of ingressing cells led to a decrease in the global level of DsRedE expression in the vesicle of the ablated side compared to the contralateral vesicle (non-ablated side: 1492 ± 58, ablated side: 454 ± 44 a.u).
source: Ablation of a limited number of cells (2–3 cells per laser pulse; see Material and methods for more details) led to a decrease in the global level of DsRedE expression (calculated as the sum of the Fcell for all neurog1+ cells) in the vesicle of the ablated side as compared to the contralateral vesicle on the non-ablated side of the embryo (Figure 4C and E; non-ablated side: 1492 ± 58, ablated side: 454 ± 44 a.u).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 4C and E

claim: Applying an increased number of laser pulses ablated more cells, which seems to lead to a more severe specification phenotype.
source: Applying an increased number of laser pulses ablated more cells, which seems to lead to a more severe specification phenotype (compare embryos 1 and 2 from Figure 4C, which received 1 and 3 laser pulses respectively), despite the overall morphology of the neurogenic domain being unaffected.
evidence: Supported by comparison of ablation phenotypes shown in Figure 4C

claim: The effect of ablation persists at 21 hpf and 42 hpf, and does not appear to represent a delay in neuronal specification.
source: Analysis of both neurog1 expression in the otic epithelium at 21 hpf and the phenotype of the SAG at 42 hpf confirms that the effect of ablation persists and, thus, does not appear to represent a delay in neuronal specification (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A,B and C; Video 12).
evidence: Supported by analysis of neurog1 expression and SAG phenotype shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A, B, C and Video 12

claim: The effect of ablation is specific to otic neurog1 expression, since DsRedE expression in the neural tube was not affected.
source: The effect of ablation is specific to otic neurog1 expression, since DsRedE expression in the neural tube was not affected (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2D

claim: Ablation of neurog1+ cells in other locations or developmental stages did not affect neurog1 expression in the otic vesicle.
source: Moreover, we observed a phenotype only after ablating anterior future ingressing cells: ablation of neurog1+ cells in another location (posterior to the placode at 13 hpf, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B) or developmental stage (anterior to the vesicle at 19 hpf, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) did not affect neurog1 expression in the otic vesicle.
evidence: Supported by ablation experiments shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and C

claim: Ablation reduced the number of neurog1+ cells in the ablated side vesicle compared to the control vesicle (non-ablated side: 23.8 ± 1.4 cells, ablated side: 10.0 ± 0.8 cells).
source: When comparing the number of neurog1+ cells (Nneurog1+), we also found a reduction in the ablated side vesicle compared to the control vesicle (Figure 4F; non-ablated side: 23.8 ± 1.4 cells, ablated side: 10.0 ± 0.8 cells).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4F

claim: The number of cells eliminated by ablation is too small to account for the large decrease in the number of neurog1+ cells in the vesicles of the ablated side.
source: Interestingly, the number of cells eliminated by ablation (and the ones produced by their divisions) would be too small to account for the large decrease in the number of neurog1+ cells in the vesicles of the ablated side (Figure 4F).
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ablated cell number and reduction in neurog1+ cells shown in Figure 4F

claim: Ingressing cells play an instructive role on the specification of other cells of the neurogenic domain.
source: This suggests that ingressing cells play an instructive role on the specification of other cells of the neurogenic domain (i.e. local specification).
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments showing reduction in neurog1+ cells beyond the number of ablated cells

claim: The number of neurog1+Hi cells was significantly lowered by ablation (non-ablated side: 6.0 ± 0.6, ablated side: 1.0 ± 0.4 cells).
source: Accordingly, the number of neurog1+Hi cells (Nneurog1+Hi) was also significantly lowered by ablation (Figure 4H; non-ablated side: 6.0 ± 0.6, ablated side: 1.0 ± 0.4 cells).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4H

claim: Most neurog1+Hi cells at 19 hpf are neurog1- cells at 13 hpf positioned inside the epithelising placode before ingression takes place, belonging to the pool of cells specified locally.
source: We discarded this possibility by backtracking cells identified as neurog1+Hi at 19 hpf from non-ablated embryos, and observing that most of them are neurog1- cells at 13 hpf positioned inside the epithelising placode before ingression takes place, therefore belonging to the pool of cells specified locally (Figure 4I and J).
evidence: Supported by backtracking analysis shown in Figures 4I and J

claim: Blocking proliferation with aphidicolin and hydroxyurea decreased the number of neurog1+ cells at 20 hpf (fold change AH/DMSO: 49.6 ± 6.3%) but the mean levels of neurog1 expression were not affected (fold change AH/DMSO: 110 ± 11%).
source: However, the effect of cell ablation was not recapitulated when proliferation was blocked by incubation with aphidicolin and hydroxyurea (AH) (Hoijman et al., 2015). This treatment decreased the number of neurog1+ cells at 20 hpf (fold change AH/DMSO: 49,6 ± 6.3%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E) but the mean levels of neurog1 expression were not affected (fold change AH/DMSO: 110 ± 11%, Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E and cited reference

claim: Cell number and expression levels are not necessarily linked during otic neurog1 expression.
source: This result suggests that cell number and expression levels are not necessarily linked during otic neurog1 expression and highlights the specific relevance of the ingressing cells in promoting the transcription of the neurog1 gene.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of ablation and proliferation inhibition experiments

claim: Pioneer neurogenic cells contribute to the neurogenic domain both through their incorporation as neurog1+ cells and by promoting neurog1 expression non-autonomously in other cells of the domain.
source: Altogether, these results indicate that these cells act as pioneer neurogenic cells, contributing to the neurogenic domain both through their incorporation as neurog1+ cells and by promoting neurog1 expression non-autonomously in other cells of the domain.
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments showing both direct and instructive contributions

claim: SU5402 treatment reduced the global level of DsRedE expression.
source: Analysis of neuronal specification indicated that SU5402 treatment reduced the global level of DsRedE expression (Figure 5C), in agreement with the previous ISH analysis of neurog1 expression (Vemaraju et al., 2012; Léger et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5C and comparison with cited references

claim: SU5402 treatment reduced the mean level of neurog1 expression in each cell and the number of neurog1+ cells, particularly neurog1+Hi cells.
source: This reduction was caused not only by a decreased mean level of neurog1 expression in each cell (Figure 5B and C), but also by a reduction in the number of neurog1+ cells (Figure 5C, and particularly in the neurog1+Hi cells).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 5B and C

claim: Inducing expression of dominant negative FGF receptor 1 at 10 hpf phenocopied the effect on otic neurog1 expression observed in SU5402 treated embryos at 20 hpf.
source: To confirm that the FGF pathway is mediating the mentioned phenotype, we crossed a transgenic line expressing a dominant negative isoform of the FGF receptor 1 fused to GFP under the control of a heat-shock (hs) promoter (hsp70:dnfgfr1-EGFP) (Norton et al., 2005) with the TgBAC(neurog1:DsRedE)nl6 line. Inducing transgene expression at 10 hpf phenocopied at 20 hpf the effect on otic neurog1 expression observed in SU5402 treated embryos (Figure 5D and E).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 5D and E and cited reference

claim: Blocking FGF signalling from 11 hpf onwards significantly reduces the number of ingressed cells (DMSO: 4.7 ± 1.1 cells, SU5402: 1.0 ± 0.4 cells; heat-shocked siblings 5.3 ± 0.4 cells; heat-shocked hsp70:dnfgfr1-EGFP/+: 0.2 ± 0.2 cells).
source: As shown in Figure 5G and I, SU5402 treatment or DNFGFR1-EGFP induction significantly reduce the number of ingressed cells (DMSO: 4.7 ± 1.1 cells, SU5402: 1.0 ± 0.4 cells; heat-shocked siblings 5,3 ± 0.4 cells; heat-shocked hsp70:dnfgfr1-EGFP/+: 0.2 ± 0.2 cells).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figures 5G and I

claim: The FGF pathway contributes to neuronal specification in the otic vesicle by promoting the ingression of the pioneer cells into the neurogenic domain.
source: These results suggest that the FGF pathway contributes to neuronal specification in the otic vesicle by promoting the ingression of the pioneer cells into the neurogenic domain.
evidence: Inferred from FGF inhibition experiments showing reduced cell ingression

claim: In DNFGFR1-EGFP expressing embryos, photoconverted cells still move towards the otic epithelium but remain outside.
source: Tracking of photoconverted cells in these embryos showed that they still move towards the otic epithelium but remain outside (Figure 5—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by tracking analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1E

claim: In DNFGFR1-EGFP expressing embryos, the anterior region of the epithelium folds at an earlier stage in development than in control embryos, becoming synchronous with folding of the posterior region.
source: Interestingly, in these embryos the anterior region of the epithelium folds at an earlier stage in development than in control embryos (Figure 5J; Video 13), becoming synchronous with folding of the posterior region (and not asynchronously as in the wild type embryos, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D; Video 8).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 5J and Video 13

claim: The otic basal lamina formed earlier in DNFGFR1-EGFP expressing embryos than in siblings.
source: Additionally, the otic basal lamina also formed earlier in DNFGFR1-EGFP expressing embryos than in siblings (Figure 5K).
evidence: Supported by laminin staining shown in Figure 5K

claim: Overexpression of FGF3 did not affect anterior events (folding and cell ingression).
source: Conversely, overexpression of FGF3 by heat-shocking a hsp70:fgf3 line did not affect the anterior events (folding and cell ingression, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G) suggesting that endogenous anterior FGF levels are sufficient to mediate these processes.
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F and G

claim: FGF3 overexpression led to a delay in folding of the posterior part of the epithelium.
source: However, this manipulation led to a delay in folding of the posterior part of the epithelium, (a region where endogenous FGFs are not acting), supporting the notion that FGFs regulate otic epithelialisation.
evidence: Supported by analysis of FGF3 overexpression experiments

claim: Endogenous FGF activity delays the final steps of anterior otic placode morphogenesis, providing time for cell ingression before the epithelial barriers appear.
source: Altogether, these results suggest that endogenous FGF activity delays the final steps of anterior otic placode morphogenesis, providing time for cell ingression before the epithelial barriers appear.
evidence: Inferred from FGF manipulation experiments showing effects on epithelialisation timing and cell ingression

claim: Blocking FGF did not modify the number of otic cells positive for phospho-Histone 3.
source: Although important in other contexts, the control of proliferation does not seem to play a central role in the FGF signalling effect on otic specification, as blocking FGF did not modify the number of otic cells positive for phospho-Histone 3 (pH3+ cells, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, A and B).
evidence: Supported by quantitative measurements shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B

claim: Pioneer otic neurogenic cells are specified outside the otic epithelium and instruct neuronal specification.
source: We have identified a new group of cells that act as pioneers of the otic neurogenic domain. These cells have two essential roles: they constitute the first specified cells of the domain and they promote specification of resident cells of the vesicle, thus spreading commitment to a neural fate (Figure 5L).
evidence: Summary of findings from ablation and tracking experiments

claim: This is the first example of neuronal progenitors instructing specification of other progenitors.
source: To our knowledge, this is the first example of neuronal progenitors instructing specification of other progenitors.
evidence: Based on comparison with existing literature

claim: In the mammalian developing brain, differentiated neurons of the cortical plate migrate to invade the dorsal telencephalon and are able to control the timing of progenitor neurogenesis.
source: In the mammalian developing brain, differentiated neurons of the cortical plate migrate to invade the dorsal telencephalon and are able to control the timing of progenitor neurogenesis (Teissier et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from published reference

claim: The SAG integrates neuronal cells from at least two different origins: the ingressing cells and the ones specified locally.
source: Our data indicate that the SAG integrates neuronal cells from at least two different origins: the ingressing cells and the ones specified locally.
evidence: Inferred from tracking and ablation experiments

claim: Different neuronal populations have been identified in the SAG, including vestibular and auditory neurons.
source: Different neuronal populations have been already identified in the SAG, including vestibular and auditory neurons (Torres and Giráldez, 1998; Bell et al., 2008).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: In chick, a transitory population of cells surrounding the invaginating otic placode was described and termed 'otic crest cells'.
source: In chick, a transitory population of cells surrounding the invaginating otic placode was described and termed 'otic crest cells' (Hemond and Morest, 1991).
evidence: Cited from published reference

claim: Ingression of cells from outside to the otic epithelium might be an evolutionarily conserved event, since it was also reported to occur during mouse otic development.
source: Moreover, ingression of cells from outside to the otic epithelium might be an evolutionarily conserved event, since it was also reported to occur during mouse otic development (Freyer et al., 2011).
evidence: Cited from published reference

claim: The otic neurogenic domain emerges in a defined ventroanterolateral position due to the dialogue of several signalling pathways that regionalise the otic placode.
source: The otic neurogenic domain emerges in a defined ventroanterolateral position due to the dialogue of several signalling pathways that regionalise the otic placode (Maier et al., 2014; Fekete and Wu, 2002; Abello and Alsina, 2007; Raft and Groves, 20142015).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: When ingressing cells are laser ablated, the cells in the otic vesicle located in the position of the ingressed cells do not seem to adopt a neurogenic fate.
source: Moreover, when ingressing cells are laser ablated, the cells in the otic vesicle located in the position of the ingressed cells (i.e. receiving the same putative diffusing morphogens) do not seem to adopt a neurogenic fate.
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments

claim: Secreted factors establish a region competent for neurogenic specification, to which the ingressing cells provide instructive signals to induce neurog1 expression.
source: This suggests that secreted factors establish a region competent for neurogenic specification, to which the ingressing cells (and probably other mechanisms) provide instructive signals to induce neurog1 expression.
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments and existing knowledge of signaling pathways

claim: Tbx1 is a repressor of neurog1 expression and is excluded from the anterior part of the vesicle, making the region competent to be induced by neurogenic signals.
source: In agreement with this possibility, Tbx1, the main transcription factor involved in otic neurogenic regionalisation, is a repressor of neurog1 expression. Tbx1 is excluded from the anterior part of the vesicle, making the region competent to be induced by neurogenic signals (Bok et al., 2011; Radosevic et al., 2011; Raft et al., 2004).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: Coordination between cell movement and cell communication contributes to the neuronal pattern of the otic vesicle.
source: Thus, in addition to the reported role of cell movements on the spatial delimitation of different domains of the neural tube (Xiong et al., 2013; Kicheva et al., 2014), we propose that coordination between cell movement and cell communication contributes to the neuronal pattern of the otic vesicle.
evidence: Inferred from findings and comparison with cited references

claim: In embryos mutant for FGF3, FGF8 and FGF10, and embryos in which FGF signalling has been temporally blocked, distinct phases of otic neural development are impaired.
source: In embryos mutant for FGF3, FGF8 and FGF10, and embryos in which FGF signalling has been temporally blocked, distinct phases of otic neural development are impaired (Wright and Mansour, 2003; Zelarayan et al., 2007; Pirvola et al., 2000; Léger et al., 2002; Vemaraju et al., 2012; Alsina et al., 2004; Alvarez et al., 2003).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: Some of the previously reported effects of FGF on neurog1 expression could be due to FGF's role in promoting ingression of pioneer cells.
source: Our work indicates that FGF signalling promotes ingression of pioneer cells into the neurogenic domain, suggesting that some of the previously reported effects on neurog1 expression could be due to this novel role.
evidence: Inferred from FGF manipulation experiments

claim: FGF signalling controls cell behaviour in other organs, such as epithelialisation and cell migration during kidney tubulogenesis and lateral line development.
source: Additionally, FGF signalling is known to control cell behaviour in other organs, such as epithelialisation and cell migration during kidney tubulogenesis and lateral line development (Atsuta and Takahashi, 2015; Aman and Piotrowski, 2008).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: FGF signalling controls epithelial invagination during otic morphogenesis in the chick.
source: Particularly in the inner ear, FGF signalling controls epithelial invagination during otic morphogenesis in the chick (Sai and Ladher, 2008).
evidence: Cited from published reference

claim: The candidate ligands for the FGF effects on morphogenesis might be FGF8 and FGF3 coming from the hindbrain and FGF3 from the endoderm and mesoderm.
source: The candidate ligands for the FGF effects on morphogenesis might be FGF8 and FGF3 coming from the hindbrain (Maves et al., 2002) and FGF3 from the endoderm and mesoderm (McCarroll and Nechiporuk, 2013).
evidence: Based on cited references describing FGF expression patterns

claim: FGF10a is not involved in otic neurogenesis processes, as neurog1 expression is normal in otic vesicles of FGF10a mutant embryos.
source: FGF10a is also expressed at these stages in the region where the pioneer cells are migrating (McCarroll and Nechiporuk, 2013). However, neurog1 expression is normal in otic vesicles of FGF10a mutant embryos (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D), indicating that this ligand is most probably not involved in these processes.
evidence: Supported by analysis of FGF10a mutant embryos shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C and D and cited reference

claim: The Notch pathway could participate in the instructive process, but the instructive signal should inhibit Notch activity in the resident cells of the vesicle.
source: The Notch pathway could participate in this process. However, since Notch activation reduces the number of specified neuronal cells via lateral inhibition (Haddon et al., 1998; Abelló et al., 2007) and ingression enhances it, the instructive signal should inhibit Notch activity in the resident cells of the vesicle.
evidence: Inferred from known Notch function and observed ingression effects, with cited references

claim: The mechanism for instruction seems to rely on the activation of the neurog1 promoter more than in stimulation of proliferation.
source: Given that inhibition of cell ingression reduced not only the number of neurog1+ cells but also the mean expression levels, the mechanism for instruction seems to rely on the activation of the neurog1 promoter more than in stimulation of proliferation.
evidence: Inferred from ablation experiments showing effects on both cell number and expression levels

claim: During the time frame analysed, no divisions were found where one daughter cell remained as a neurog1- progenitor while the other activated the proneural expression.
source: During the time frame analysed, no divisions were found where one daughter cell remained as a neurog1- progenitor while the other activated the proneural expression, as has been described in the neural tube (Wilcock et al., 2007; Das and Storey, 2012; Taverna et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by direct observation in time-lapse imaging data, with comparison to cited references

claim: Studies of fixed chick otic vesicles described the presence of mitosis in the basal side of the epithelium in addition to the luminal ones, termed 'basal divisions'.
source: Studies of fixed chick otic vesicles described the presence of mitosis in the basal side of the epithelium in addition to the luminal ones (Alvarez et al., 1989). Such mitoses were termed 'basal divisions' similar to the ones taking place in the retina in which mitotic cells are no longer polarized apically and in contact with the ventricular membrane (Weber et al., 2014).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: Non-luminal mitoses remain in contact with a Pard3 scaffold and therefore still keep their apical polarity.
source: In our study, we also observed non-luminal mitoses, but our data show that these divisions remain in contact with a Pard3 scaffold and therefore still keep their apical polarity.
evidence: Supported by Pard3 localization data

claim: Stable cell-cell contacts would be dispensable to initiate proneural expression.
source: Neural specification usually occurs in epithelialised tissues. However, we observed activation of neurog1 expression in pioneer cells before epithelialisation, suggesting that stable cell-cell contacts would be dispensable to initiate proneural expression.
evidence: Inferred from observation of neurog1 activation before epithelialisation

claim: In mouse, neurog2 is expressed in migrating sensory neuron precursors, although its expression begins before exiting the epithelium and migration.
source: Similarly, in mouse neurog2 is expressed in migrating sensory neuron precursors (Marmigère and Ernfors, 2007), although its expression begins before exiting the epithelium and migration (Zirlinger et al., 2002).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: Delamination occurs once a given threshold of proneural expression is reached, probably associated to neurod1 induction.
source: Analysis of neurog1 expression levels suggests that delamination occurs once a given threshold of proneural expression is reached; probably associated to neurod1 induction.
evidence: Inferred from quantitative analysis of neurog1 expression levels at delamination

claim: The otic placode and other cranial placodes originate from a large common pre-placodal region (PPR) adjacent to the neural plate.
source: The otic placode and other cranial placodes originate from a large common pre-placodal region (PPR) adjacent to the neural plate (Bailey and Streit, 20052006).
evidence: Cited from published reference

claim: Precursors from the PPR segregate and coalesce into individual cranial placodes, which progressively acquire specific identities.
source: Precursors from the PPR segregate and coalesce into individual cranial placodes, which progressively acquire specific identities (Breau and Schneider-Maunoury, 2014; Streit, 2002; Bhat and Riley, 2011; Saint-Jeannet and Moody, 2014; McCarroll et al., 2012).
evidence: Cited from published references

claim: Neural specification might precede the acquisition of a defined placodal identity.
source: Our data revealed that otic neurog1 is expressed before of what it was conceived and outside the epithelium by a group of cells that ingress during morphogenesis. This suggests that neural specification might precede the acquisition of a defined placodal identity.
evidence: Inferred from observation of neurog1 expression outside the otic epithelium

claim: Some PPR precursors might already be committed to a neural fate and their subsequent allocation into the placodes provides them one or another placodal identity.
source: Thus, we propose that some PPR precursors might already be committed to a neural fate and that their subsequent allocation into the placodes (by random or directed movements) provides them one or another placodal identity.
evidence: Speculative proposal based on findings of early neurog1 expression
